content: Asthma is a widespread chronic condition globally, and inhalers are commonly prescribed to manage symptoms, enhance quality of life, and reduce the risk of exacerbations. However, research indicates that many individuals with asthma do not use their inhalers correctly. This highlights the importance of evaluating whether interventions designed to improve inhaler technique are both effective and safe, and whether these interventions lead to better clinical outcomes. The objective of this review was to assess the impact of interventions aimed at improving inhaler technique on clinical outcomes and safety in both adults and children with asthma. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, trial registries, and reference lists of primary studies, with the most recent search completed on November 23, 2016. The review included studies that compared groups receiving inhaler technique interventions with those receiving control or alternative interventions. Both parallel and cluster-randomized trials of any duration were included, as well as the first phase of any cross-over trials. Studies were eligible regardless of whether they were published as full-text articles, abstracts, or unpublished data. Two reviewers independently screened the search results for eligible studies, extracted outcome data, and assessed the risk of bias. Discrepancies were resolved by involving a third reviewer. Studies with similar comparisons were grouped, and meta-analyses were conducted when the treatments, participants, and clinical questions were sufficiently similar. Dichotomous data were analyzed using odds ratios, while continuous data were analyzed using mean differences or standardized mean differences, all within random-effects models. Skewed data were described narratively. The quality of evidence was graded, and findings were summarized in tables. The primary outcomes assessed were inhaler technique, asthma control, and exacerbations requiring oral corticosteroids. The review included 29 parallel randomized controlled trials involving 2,210 participants, although not all studies provided relevant or usable data. Participants had asthma, and follow-up periods ranged from 2 to 26 weeks. Most studies had a low or unclear risk of selection and attrition biases but were at high risk for biases related to blinding. The overall quality of evidence was considered low due to these biases and imprecision in effect estimates. The studies were categorized into three types of interventions: enhanced face-to-face training sessions, multimedia-delivered inhaler training (e.g., DVDs, computer applications, or games), and technique feedback devices. Differences in interventions, populations, and outcome measures limited the ability to perform quantitative analyses, particularly for outcomes such as exacerbations, adverse events, unscheduled healthcare visits, and absenteeism from work or school. Enhanced inhaler technique education and multimedia training improved inhaler technique in most studies, both immediately after the intervention and at follow-up. However, the variety of checklists used to assess technique made it challenging to reliably evaluate these improvements. The timing and method of inhaler technique assessment influenced the extent of improvement observed. Analyses focusing on the number of individuals demonstrating correct or good enough technique were generally more informative than checklist scores. For adults, enhanced education showed significant benefits when correct technique was assessed at follow-up periods ranging from 2 to 26 weeks. For example, one analysis found that 31% of participants in the control group demonstrated correct technique compared to 69% in the education group (odds ratio [OR] 5.00, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.83 to 13.65; moderate-quality evidence). Similarly, feedback devices showed benefits at four weeks' follow-up, with 51% of participants in the control group demonstrating correct technique compared to 83% in the feedback group (OR 4.80, 95% CI 1.87 to 12.33; low-quality evidence). However, the benefit of multimedia training for adults was less certain, even immediately after the intervention (OR 2.15, 95% CI 0.84 to 5.50; moderate-quality evidence). For children, the evidence was less clear, often due to fewer and smaller studies. Some studies did not report exacerbations in a way that allowed for meta-analysis, while others provided inconclusive results. Interventions to improve inhaler technique showed some benefits for asthma control and quality of life but generally did not result in consistent or clinically significant improvements for either adults or children. Confidence intervals often included no difference or did not reach thresholds considered clinically important. Responder analyses occasionally showed improvements among more individuals in the intervention groups, even when the mean difference between groups was small. No evidence was found regarding potential harms associated with these interventions. In conclusion, while interventions to improve inhaler technique may be effective in certain circumstances, the diversity of interventions and measurement methods limited the ability to perform meta-analyses and reduced confidence in the findings. Most studies did not report significant improvements in clinical outcomes. Current guidelines recommend that clinicians regularly check their patients' inhaler technique, but it remains unclear how best to intervene when technique is inadequate and whether such interventions will lead to meaningful clinical benefits.
